units.translation: b. And fair through its mouth: the Ister has three mouths, of which one is called the Fair Mouth, as Timagetus says in his work On Harbours (fr. 2 M. IV 519); into this he says Apsyrtus sailed.
c. 〈mouth:〉 of the Ister. Gᶢ Sᵐ
308a. uttermost of the Ionian sea: the Ionian sea is off Italy, into which the Adriatic discharges; therefore some call it the Adriatic.
b. The Ionian sea is so called near Italy. It was named after Ionius, an Illyrian by birth, as Theopompus says in his twenty-first book (115 fr. 128a J.); but some say from the wandering of Io.

310. three-pronged: Eratosthenes in the third book of his Geography (fr. III B 98 Berger) says that there is a triangular island in the Ister, equal in size to Rhodes, which is called Peuce because it has many pine trees.

311-14. And on both sides two: around the bend near Peuce he says there are two mouths of the Ister, of which one is called Narex, the other the Fair Mouth, by which the Colchians with Apsyrtus sailed more quickly.

315-18a. But they high above the island: those with Jason sailed from above the island through the mouth of Narex. But the herdsmen, thinking that the ships—all of them, one must understand—were sea monsters, took fright and turned to flight. L
b. Meadows are low-lying, marshy places. One must understand that the herdsmen fled on both sides. L
320a. Neither then with the Thracians: the Scythians are neighbours to the Thracians in Europe.
b. 〈nor the Sigynni: . . .〉 There is also a sigynnus, a kind of spear, named after the tribe.

321-22. Nor those around Laurium: Laurium is a plain of Scythia. Timonax in the first book of his work On Scythians (fr. 1 M. IV 522) records fifty-five tribes of Scythia. 〈. . .〉 At the plain of the Sindi the river Ister divides, and one stream of it flows into the Adriatic, the other into the Euxine Sea. Herodian in the sixth book of his General Prosody (I 142, 20 L.) says that the word Sindi should be barytone; but some make it oxytone, incorrectly. Hipponax (fr. 68 A B. II 484) also mentions it, with reference to the 'Sindic strait'. Hellanicus in his work On Peoples says (4 fr. 69 J.): 'After crossing the Bosporus one comes to the Sindi, and above them the Maeotian Scythians'.

323-26a. Of the Angurum mountain: Angurum is a mountain near the river Ister. Timagetus mentions it in his work On Harbours (fr. 5 M. IV 520). The Cauliacan rock is in Scythia near the Ister, which Polemon mentions in his Foundations of Italian and Sicilian Cities (fr. 38 M. III 126). It is written [Angurum mountain] also as Agtyrum mountain and Angyri mountain, and instead of Cauliacan: Caucaean. He says that at this mountain the Ister divides and one stream flows into the Adriatic, the other into the Euxine.
b. 〈Caucaean:〉 it is written Cauliacan. Lᶢ
327. Cronian sea: he means the Adriatic; for there they say Cronus dwelt.
